newsitem.title: GHANA: After showcase Ghana polls, focus turns to economy.
newsitem.headline: After showcase Ghana polls, focus turns to economy.

text.p: The re-election of Jerry Rawlings as president of Ghana has sent a strong democratic signal to Africa and won praise from investors seeking stability.

But foreign businessmen said on Thursday it remained to be seen whether Rawlings would embrace some of the more business-oriented policies of his main opposition rival, lawyer-businessman John Kufuor.
The national elections commission on Wednesday proclaimed the results of last Saturday's presidential and parliamentary elections, giving Rawlings an emphatic win in both.

Rawlings polled 57 percent in the presidential election, against 39 percent for Kufuor, becoming the first incumbent to be re-elected in Ghana, the country which he has dominated politically for 15 years.
"We the foreign business community are delighted with the way the elections went," said the head of a large Western company in Accra, who asked not to be named.
"And I happen to know that local businessmen urged Kufuor to accept defeat and congratulate Rawlings. They want to build, develop, do business. Reason and pragmatism triumphed," he said.
Canadian gold miner Kevin Bullock said, "Everybody in the industry is happy with this outcome. With President Rawlings we know what to expect.

"Under Rawlings the 1987 mining act came into existence. That is a very modern act. It continues bringing in a lot of foreign investors. If you find a gold mine in West Africa, it is a big bonus if you find it in Ghana."
Many Ghanaians irrespective of how they voted, appear genuinely proud of staging one of the smoothest elections in a region where organisational shortcomings have often led to poll violence.

Ghana pioneered independence from colonial rule in West Africa in 1957 and Ghanaians have long cherished the image of pacesetters. Ghana again led the region in economic reforms, started by Rawlings over a decade ago.

"We are aware that we are blazing a trail in Africa," said Joe Abbey, a former finance minister who now heads Ghana's Centre for Policy Analysis. "Ghanaians are aware of the dangers of civil strife. They will not be willing to throw away what they have been building for over 15 years."
In the runup to the elections, the opposition raised doubts about Rawlings's liberal credentials and many local business leaders had their worries.
Rawlings managed to win support from young business executives, the main beneficiaries of growth and the economic reforms inspired by the International Monetary Fund.
But many local investors have not been completely at home with Rawlings' past image. They say his National Democratic Congress party has kept a populist edge, a legacy of its Rawling's past.
Many Ghanaians believe Rawlings has much to learn from Kufuor's advocacy of gradualist liberalisation that favours Ghanaian investors rather than foreign capital.
Despite winning praise from donors for economic reform, the pain of adjustment is a touchy political issue as shown by bloody riots in Accra last year over value-added tax.
In his victory remarks, Rawlings spoke of getting all hands on deck to build Ghana. Many industry analysts hope he does not exclude Kufuor.
Leading economists say he needs all the help he can get to stabilise the macroeconomic environment.

"Macroeconomic stability has suffered a setback in recent years. Fluctuations are too big. In one year inflation has moved from 20 to 70 percent and back again. That is not a tenable situation," Abbey said.

"Too much of the instability can be traced to budgetary or fiscal imbalances. The real task is how to get government finance right," Abbey said. "In 1995 government did not pay all its bills. Nevertheless growth of money supply was 37 percent."
Average money supply growth since 1990 has been 40 percent.
Optimists expect Rawlings to use his mandatory final four-year term to leave a legacy for Ghana. "I think that that legacy will be his willingness to take tough choices on the economy," Abbey said.
